title: Triple Crown One Day, 'Human Circle' Security Scandal The Next — Hearts2Hearts' Wild Week
excerpt: SM Entertainment's hottest rookie group Hearts2Hearts clinched a triple crown with 'RUDE!' on March 19 — then sparked a massive debate after bodyguards formed a literal hand-holding ring around them at Incheon Airport. 'Even the president doesn't get that level of security,' netizens said.
author: MEARROW Editorial Desk
content:
The euphoria from a triple crown barely lasted 24 hours before a different kind of viral moment took over.

On March 19, SM Entertainment's girl group **Hearts2Hearts** secured a triple crown win for "RUDE!" on M! Countdown. It marked another milestone for the group crowned 'Monster Rookies' after sweeping seven rookie-of-the-year awards in their debut year. Then, the very next day, footage from Incheon International Airport set off a completely different conversation.

## Who Are Hearts2Hearts?

Hearts2Hearts (Korean: 하츠투하츠) is an eight-member girl group under SM Entertainment, debuted on February 24, 2025. The members — Carmen, Jiwoo, Yuha, Stella, Juun, A-na, Ian, and Ye-on — represent multiple nationalities, with Indonesian member Carmen making history as SM Entertainment's first Indonesian idol.

Their debut year was nothing short of a sprint. In 2025 alone, they swept rookie honors at MAMA, the Hanteo Music Awards, the Golden Disc Awards, and the Korea Grand Music Awards, amassing seven rookie-of-the-year trophies. They entered 2026 with the "Monster Rookies" label firmly in place and a Japanese market expansion already underway.

## "RUDE!" Triple Crown: The Breakdown

**"RUDE!"** dropped on February 20, 2026, as a pre-release single ahead of Hearts2Hearts' second mini album. Described by SM as a "rule-breaking" house pop track, the music video used a 'heart factory' metaphor to explore authenticity in a world saturated with "fake likes." The song peaked at **#11 on the Billboard K-pop Hot 100** in March.

The music show chart race unfolded quickly:

| Date | Show | Result |
|------|------|--------|
| March 5 | M! Countdown | 1st win |
| March 14 | Show! Music Core | 2nd win |
| March 19 | M! Countdown | **Triple crown** |

Notably, the March 19 triple crown was achieved **without the group performing on the show**. The win came purely from fan streaming and digital performance — which fans celebrated as a demonstration of fandom power standing on its own.

![Hearts2Hearts RUDE! Triple Crown and Incheon Airport Security Controversy](/images/news/hearts2hearts-triple-crown-rude-incheon-airport-security-2026-thumbnail.webp)

## March 18, Incheon Airport — The "Ganggangsullae Security" Footage

One day before the triple crown, on March 18, footage from Incheon International Airport began circulating online.

The videos showed **multiple bodyguards holding hands to form a circular formation around the Hearts2Hearts members** as they moved through the airport toward the departure gates. The visual immediately drew comparisons to *Ganggangsullae* — a traditional Korean circle folk dance where participants hold hands in a ring — and the label "Ganggangsullae Security" stuck almost instantly.

The footage spread rapidly, and reactions split sharply.

## The Backlash: "Even the President Doesn't Get That"

Critics organized around three main complaints.

**"The scale is excessive."** The most widely shared comment across online communities: "Even the president doesn't get that level of security." The sight of an idol group moving through a public airport inside a hand-held human ring struck many as disproportionate — an image more commonly associated with head-of-state protection details than entertainment management.

**"Blocking public pathways crosses a line."** Video footage included moments where regular airport travelers were visibly forced to detour or halt in place to accommodate the security formation. Critics argued that celebrity protection cannot reasonably extend to impeding other people's right to move through public infrastructure.

**"Poor advance planning."** Despite SM Entertainment having filed an advance airport use plan, observers noted that the on-the-ground execution still produced significant crowding and inconvenience.

## The Defense: "What Else Are They Supposed to Do?"

Those defending the security approach were equally vocal.

**"Overzealous fans create real physical risk."** Airports are not controlled environments. When dozens to hundreds of fans converge on an idol group in a transit corridor, the risk of physical incidents — trampling, aggressive contact, collapsed crowd situations — is real, for both the artists and bystanders. The circular formation, supporters argued, was a practical barrier, not a vanity project.

**"SM followed procedure."** The agency submitted the required advance plan to airport authorities. The problem, some argued, is not that SM ignored process, but that the process itself is insufficient.

**"Blame the fans, not the formation."** Several commenters pointed out that holding bodyguards to impossible standards while ignoring the crowd behavior that makes those formations necessary was logically backwards.

## Airport Authority's Response: "We Can't Give Everyone Fast-Track"

As the controversy grew, Incheon International Airport officials addressed the incident directly.

> "Not all entertainers can be given fast-track access. It is difficult to establish objective criteria for such a system."

This response revealed an important contextual layer: SM had reportedly requested fast-track passage for the members, which airport authorities declined. Lacking that option, security staff defaulted to the circular hand-holding formation as their best available solution through standard terminal pathways.

The structural gap is the actual story. Korean celebrity airport traffic has created recurring congestion issues for years, but no formal system — fast-track tiering, dedicated celebrity lanes, mandatory advance coordination with terminal security — has been institutionalized.

## What This Moment Actually Reveals

The "Ganggangsullae security" controversy is not, at its core, about whether the formation looked excessive.

It is about the widening gap between the scale at which K-pop now operates and the infrastructure that surrounds it. Hearts2Hearts is a group that debuted fourteen months ago. They are already at a point where moving through a public airport without a human ring around them is genuinely complicated. That is not a PR problem. That is a consequence of a machine — fandom culture, agency promotion, social media virality — that has grown faster than the systems meant to manage its effects.

The fact that this footage emerged the same week as a triple crown is almost too on the nose. Hearts2Hearts, in the span of 48 hours, produced a chart achievement that any established group would covet, and a visual that encapsulates everything uncomfortable about how K-pop idols now exist in public space.

SM Entertainment had not issued a formal statement on the airport security approach as of publication.

Triple crown. Human circle. That is March 2026 for Hearts2Hearts in two images.
